news_drafts.headline: Newcastle ended 2025-26 with a £0.483m underspend against a budget of about £1.2bn
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle City Council finished the 2025-26 financial year with an underspend of £0.483m, according to a performance report going to its Corporate Scrutiny Committee on 8 October. The figure is the outturn, meaning the actual result for the year once it had ended, as against what was budgeted. It is about 0.04% of a budget of roughly £1.2bn.

The £1.2bn covers the council's General Fund (its main budget for running services), its housing revenue account (the separate, ring-fenced account for council-owned homes, paid for by rents) and its capital programme (planned spending on things that last, such as buildings and roads).

The report says the 2025-26 final-quarter outturn "was presented to Cabinet in June, setting out a year-end underspend position of £0.483 million". The material available does not break the figure down by service or say what produced it.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle schools-funding deficit forecast to reach £17.153m by March 2027, with override extended to 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle City Council expects the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £17.153m by the end of 2026-27, according to the first-quarter outturn report (the forecast of the year's actual figures) put to Cabinet on 21 September. The grant is projecting an overspend of £11.297m this year, on top of a negative balance of £5.808m at 1 April 2026.

The overspend is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending there is forecast at £66.6m against funding of £55.2m. The paper puts spending growth at 15%, against 7% growth in funding.

For now the deficit does not touch the council's main budget. A statutory override (a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet) lets the council record it as an unusable reserve. The override was due to expire in March 2026, and the government has extended it to March 2028. The government is also offering a High Needs Stability Grant, covering up to 90% of eligible deficits, but it depends on the Department for Education approving a plan to reform support for children with special educational needs.

findings.headline: A167(M) Central Motorway £9 million improvement project progressing ahead of schedule with substantial completion expected by end of October 2026.
findings.detail: The £9 million A167(M) Central Motorway improvement programme, which began one year ago, is delivering 'critical repairs progressing ahead of schedule' with 'substantial completion now expected by the end of October 2026'. The project is also generating wider community benefits including 'local apprenticeships, student placements, volunteering initiatives and support for grassroots sports clubs'.
findings.matters: Early delivery of major capital projects demonstrates project management capability and reduces financing burden, cost risk and technical risk exposure; ahead-of-schedule delivery is rare in local authority capital programmes and suggests realistic planning and effective risk management.
findings.figures: £9 million capital investment; completion expected October 2026 (ahead of original schedule)
findings.quote: It is one year since work began on our £9 million A167(M) Central Motorway improvement programme, with critical repairs progressing ahead of schedule and substantial completion now expected by the end of October 2026. As well as futureproofing one of the city's busiest transport routes, the project is delivering wider community benefits through local apprenticeships, student placements, volunteering initiatives and support for grassroots sports clubs.

findings.headline: Council tax in-year collection improved to 28.1% from 27.5%; business rates to 31.7% from 29.1%; sundry debt to 90.4% exceeding target.
findings.detail: Council tax in-year collection at end of June was 28.1%, up 0.6pp year-on-year, with the improvement attributed to 'amendments to the student exemptions process following changes introduced by the Renters' Rights Act'. Business rates in-year collection reached 31.7%, up 2.6pp from 29.1% in June 2025, though the council notes 'legislative changes introduced on 1 April 2026 delayed some bills, resulting in some businesses receiving instalment schedules running from June 2026 to March 2027'. Sundry debt collection reached 90.4%, exceeding the 90% target for 'the first time this has exceeded the target in several months'.
findings.matters: Collection performance protects in-year cash flow and reduces bad-debt provisions; however improvements are driven by process and legislative changes rather than underlying collection behaviour, and mid-year rates of 28-31% still leave substantial collection risk in the second half as instalments fall due.
findings.figures: Council tax 28.1% vs 27.5% (June 2025); Business rates 31.7% vs 29.1% (June 2025); Sundry debt 90.4% vs 89.3%
findings.quote: Council Tax in-year collection rate (higher is better) 28.1% ... 27.5% (June 2025) Increasing / better than target; Business rates in-year collection was 31.7% at the end of June ... 31.7% ... 29.1% (June 2025) Increasing / better than target; Collection of sundry income within 90 days at the end of Quarter 1 was 90.4%, an improvement of 1.4% and the first time this has exceeded the target in several months.

findings.headline: Year-end 2025-26 outturn recorded underspend of £0.483 million—0.04% of £1.2 billion annual budget.
findings.detail: The 2025-26 Quarter 4 outturn, presented to Cabinet in June, recorded a year-end underspend of £0.483 million across a budget of approximately £1.2 billion. This represents only 0.04% contingency and indicates tight financial management with minimal buffer to absorb in-year cost pressures, demand shocks or inflation.
findings.matters: An underspend of less than £0.5m on a £1.2bn budget provides no meaningful financial contingency; it reinforces the council's vulnerability to the RED-rated financial sustainability risk and suggests the council has limited capacity to absorb unexpected costs or rising demand.
findings.figures: £0.483 million underspend; annual budget approximately £1.2 billion (General Fund, HRA and Capital Programme combined)
findings.quote: The 2025-26 Quarter 4 outturn was presented to Cabinet in June, setting out a year-end underspend position of £0.483 million.

findings.headline: Change and Innovation Newcastle Transformation Programme added as new AMBER strategic risk, with concern it may not achieve intended cross-council impact.
findings.detail: A new AMBER risk (priority 9) has been added to the strategic risk register for the Transformation Programme, flagging that 'without sustained stakeholder alignments, sufficient resourcing and a clear scope the Change and Innovation Newcastle Programme may not achieve its intended cross-council transformational impact on customer experience, service effectiveness and long-term financial sustainability.' This is the only new risk flagged in this quarter.
findings.matters: Transformation programmes are high-risk and high-cost; an AMBER flag in early delivery signals projected financial benefits and service improvements may not materialise, creating risk of sunk costs if the programme is paused or re-scoped, and leaving structural financial pressures unresolved.
findings.figures: AMBER priority 9; Direction of travel: New risk
findings.quote: Transformation Programme: There is a risk that, without sustained stakeholder alignments, sufficient resourcing and a clear scope the Change and Innovation Newcastle Programme may not achieve its intended cross-council transformational impact on customer experience, service effectiveness and long-term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Planning application processing performance declining across all timescales: major 83% vs 100%, minor 81% vs 94%, other 74% vs 85% within targets.
findings.detail: All three planning processing measures show material deterioration: major applications determined within 13 weeks fell from 100% to 83%; minor applications within 8 weeks fell from 94% to 81%; other applications within 8 weeks fell from 85% to 74%. The council notes these are statutory reporting measures and aims to 'support local economic growth' through timely processing.
findings.matters: Planning delays signal either staffing gaps or application volume surge; they deter inward investment, increase developer costs and trigger appeals and legal challenges that increase the council's future exposure and cost; sustained delays can lead to inspector intervention and loss of control over local planning decisions.
findings.figures: Major: 83% vs 100%; Minor: 81% vs 94%; Other: 74% vs 85%
findings.quote: % of major applications determined within 13 weeks (higher is better) 83% ... 100% ... Decreasing; % of minor applications determined within 8 weeks (higher is better) 81% ... 94% ... Decreasing; % of other applications determined within 8 weeks 74% 85% Decreasing
